review_notes: I read the whole target file. I also read the nsmulPt definition in Def_CerednikDrinfeld_QMModuli.lean and grepped for other statements of the nsmulPt/nsmul equality. I did not check the long `attribute [-simp]` list at line 8 against its simp lemmas, so I can't say whether any of those lemmas compete. The two scoped simp lemmas lift_ι and lift_str look fine: they have a clear orientation and the hypothesis hP is a Prop argument. The proof still uses `rw` for them, which is a style choice, not a defect. I could not run Lean, so the finding rests on repeated statements of the lemma and on how it is used with `rw`. findings.excerpt: CerednikDrinfeld.QM.nsmulPt L t k P = L.nsmul t k P := by
findings.problem: The bridge between the two spellings of n-fold multiples, `nsmulPt` and `RelativeGroupLaw.nsmul`, is proved here as a private-style helper. Nothing in the simp interface supplies it. The statement is reproved under the same name or a near-identical one in at least three other solution files. The solution proof then converts by hand with `rw [← TSLU.nsmulPt_eq_nsmul]; exact hσ`, and it does this twice (hσ' and hτ'). The target can't be handled by `simp`: `nsmulPt` is a bare recursive def with no unfolding or normal-form lemma next to its definition. Hypotheses stated with `nsmulPt` (as in FakeEllipticCurve.torsion) therefore can't be normalised to the `L.nsmul` form that the kernel API (`schemeKer`, `lift`, `coe_nsmul_eq_comp_schemeNsmul`) uses.
findings.proposed_change: State `nsmulPt_eq_nsmul` once, next to `def nsmulPt` in Definitions/Def_CerednikDrinfeld_QMModuli.lean, oriented `nsmulPt L t n P = L.nsmul t n P`. This direction has `L.nsmul` as the canonical normal form, and the right side contains no `nsmulPt`, so it cannot cycle. Consider tagging it `@[simp]`. Then delete the four local copies. The conversions in `solution` become `have hσ' : E.L.nsmul (𝟙 _) m σ = E.L.one (𝟙 _) := by simpa [nsmulPt_eq_nsmul] using hσ`. If the library keeps `nsmulPt` as a separate normal form, it should say so, and make the reverse conversion the single shared lemma.
findings.benefit: One canonical lemma replaces five copies, and users no longer need manual `rw [← …]` bridging. Hypotheses written with `nsmulPt` can be normalised by `simp` to the form the kernel API expects.
